sections.content:
(the content is just copy from the next review below me, ths that bro.)
Chronological order:
1. Complex numbers, geometric construction, polynomials and its roots.
2. Rings and Fields of numbers.
3. Groups and monoids.
4. Group actions, co-sets and orbit-stabilizer theorem.
5. Rings and fields, polynomial rings, field extensions.
6. Normal subgroup, automorphism of fields, automorphic field extension, Galois theory.
—————————————————
Midterm covered chapter 1-3 while final covered chapter 1-6, where Galois theory is not tested.

The course structure is designed to “wrap up” the problems we noticed in part 1, I.e. finding roots for quintic equations, angle tri-section problems. We build up the tools from part 2-6 to answer part 1.
Personal opinion: context is shallow and routine-work for a 3-thousand level math course. Also, I come to this course just for a good grade, but actually this course is not enough to learn abstract algebra better. At least, for PM student, they should learn http://more.To find the in-depth (or perhaps regular) abstract algebra that prepares you, go to MATH3131 that opens in spring.

sections.content:
Maybe too easy for MATH/PHY students but just right for COMP students who just want a ＊gentle introduction＊ to Abstract Algebra which is essential to reading papers in cryptography (Swartz–Zippel lemma, RSA, lattice-based cryptography). Moreover, there're many computationally hard problems like quadratic residue, diophantine equation (Hilbert's tenth problem)
in this field of interest to us. If you're COMP, this will not be counted towards your MCGA but I still recommend to at least know the basics.

In this course you'll understand many important results and their proof e.g. gcd(r,s) is also the smallest positive integer combination of r,s ; Lagrange theorem which gives a relationship between size of subgroup and the group size ; Chinese remainder theorem which gives an isomorphism ; the fundamental homomorphism theorem which gives an isomorphism between the quotient group and the range

You may also be asked to prove some smaller results like for finite cyclic group G = <g> of size m then <g^k> = <g^gcd(k,m)>

Indeed this course is Abstract in the sense that we prove results that hold in ＊general＊ instead of only working for a particular example.

fun fact: math students at Oxford take this in year 1
sections.teaching:
Prof. Chang is good teacher, your life will be much easier if you go to lecture (or watch his video) before reading lecture notes. Also he gave more examples and proofs not mentioned at all in the note e.g. proving phi(mn) = phi(m)phi(n) for coprime m,n. His explanations are easy to follow and beginner friendly.

He also gives interesting anecdotes like 「韩信点兵」when talking about Chinese remainder theorem and the author (and his students) of his favorite book on number theory being terribly bullied during revolution in China.

The TAs are also very great people, especially TA ZHANG Huaigong. He replies email fast and is helpful. Prof probably left most of the organizational and grading work to him (including giving letter grades !). A funny thing is that during final paper checking he said our exam is too easy, he can come up with the idea for each question with at most 30 sec lol I'm just too stupid

Textbook: A first course in abstract algebra by J.B. Fraleigh.
The exams covers sections 1,4,5,6,8,9,10,11,13,14,16, 18,19,20,26
I think it was little bit too easy as an abstract algebra course, so I give a B here.
sections.teaching: Prof. Chang is the best Math teacher I met in UST. He is able to present all the definitions and theorems on the whiteboard in a clear manner. His teaching really keeps you focus and is never too slow or too fast. He always remembers to remind you some important concepts in case you forget it. Moreover, he speaks very decent English. He is willing to answer questions in either English or Mandarin. I strongly suggest you to attend his lectures and thus you do not need to study any other materials for this course.
sections.grading:
Homework: 25%

Quiz: 20%. It was actually midterm. It was very easy. The average score was 29.5/40.

Final: 55%. lt was easy before the last 3 questions, each of which worths 10 points. I suggest you to do some finite field problems and this may help you to prepare for that.

The professor did not release his grading scheme. I got 93 in total, while the highest is 97. It turned out to be an A+. I think this is fair enough.
sections.workload: Very light. 6 HW sets in total, and each can be finished within an hour.

sections.content:
The course is all about groups (Ring is a kind of group, field is a kind of ring also so field is also a kind of group), and probably some kind of discrete math stuffs (Euler's formula, little Fermat's theorem).

He also offered 3 additional lectures on Jordan canonical form, polynomial ring and field theory. I think these 3 lecture are more interesting than the regular lecture.
sections.teaching:
To be fair, his teaching is really not that bad. I don't understand why you guys think his teaching is bad.

He is very kind that would answer students' question after class even if the question is quite stupid. Also, he gives plenty of the examples during the lecture time to make our understanding better. And yes, he gives us review on previous lecture so that I can catch up contents in last lecture.
sections.grading:
Grading is actually quite good that I can give an A.

Everything got median but still able to get a B.

That's quite a good grade when compared with other math courses.

Grading policy:

25% HW
75% Final + Quiz (It is actually midterm)

The percentage distribution of final and quiz will be decided one day during lecture time. It is usually 25% of quiz and 50% of final.
sections.workload:
Not heavy I would say.

If you want to get for a B-range only, then you do not need to do that much practice. Just understanding the concept and doing assignments will be enough since most of the exam question are similar, or even the same, as the homework question. Yongchang himself also said it is not difficult to get a B-range.

Do note that he will test something that is not covered in lecture notes so please go to lectures if you wish to get high marks. (He asked us to give 5 examples of subfield of R in final exam, where subfield is covered in one of the lecture, but not is lecture notes).

sections.content:
See above.

Mainly talked about
- groups, symmetric groups, group actions, rings, fields,
- group/ring homomorphism and isomorphisms
- homomorphism theorem (but none of the isomorphism theorems) for groups and rings
- some other miscellaneous subjects (not even assessed)

Pretty lackluster for a supposedly "Abstract Algebra" course (I learned more about Groups by myself in summer than in this course). This feels more like an introduction, and MATH3131 is probably the real one that you should take if you can.

4 weeks intensive classes. But...I guess most of us are deadline fighter even in regular semester? So finishing the course in short period can maintain our motivation right? SO I love summer semester more than regular semester :D

About workload...it depends on how you define "HIGH". I attended most of the class and jot notes, and spend ~2 days (you dun hv time to do more than that, and personally I dun like to do exercises or past paper...but I guess in regular sem, I would be more deadline fighter since I also hv other courses workload...) for revision for quiz/exam every week. I do the hw every week for about 4 hours. I think I work really hard and spend many time on this course, and I won't have so much time to do so in regular sem...but still fair workload!!!
(HAHA I keep encouraging people take course in summer/winter sem! )

But the bad things is...the time crush with other common core is very serious, so you won't have chance to take other common core/course when you take this course :D (Look at the schedule and you will understand :( )

sections.content:
The content is very brief but comprehensive. Here is the schedule for summer:

Week one Tu:
Basic set theory, mappings, equivalence relations (section 0)
Complex numbers and binary operations (sections 1 and 2)
Integers mod n
Groups and subgroups (section 4)

Week one Th/F:
Subgroups (section 5)
Classification of subgroups of the integers
Cyclic groups (sections 6 and 7)
Permutations groups, cycles (sections 8 and 9)
Week two M/Tu:
Cosets, Lagrange's Theorem and order of elements (section 10)
Direct products (section 11)
Homomorphisms, kernel, normal subgroup (section 13)
Quotient groups (section 14 and section 15)

Week two Th/F: Thursday (June 28):
Rings, ring homomorphism, kernel, fields (section 18)
Quotient rings (section 26)
Classification of ideals of the integers
Integers mod n as a quotient ring
Greatest common divisor of two integers and the Euclidean algorithm

Week three Tu:
Units in a ring
Prime integers and finite fields
Euler phi-function

Week three Th/F:
Fermat and Euler Theorems (section 20)
Chinese Remainder Theorem
RSA encryption
Midterm (Friday July 06 afternoon)

Week four M/Tu:
1st isomorphism theorems for groups, and rings (section 34)
Unique factorization in the integers Z
The polynomial ring F[x] (section 22)
Ideals in the polynomial ring F[x]

Week four Th/F:
The analogy of the polynomials F[x] with the integers Z
More finite fields
Symmetries (section 12)

Week five M/Tu:
Group actions, orbits, and isotropy/stabilzer subgroup (section 16)
Examples
Orbit stablizer theorem and Counting (section 17)

Week five Th/F:
Counting (section 17)
Examples
Review

In fact, since there are some "Advanced" student in this class, profssor taught more content than that, such as Gaussian numbers and Sylow Theorem.
sections.teaching:
Professor has handwritten notes for us. But in the class, he changed the order and added more example. So it's better to take the class rather than studying it by yourself.

TA is quite good and helpful. He will hand out exercises every tutorial and tries to recap what we have learned. His exercises are extracted from textbook but really can help students get familiar with the course concepts.
sections.grading:
The grading is absolute grading.
66% from exams   =   26% Midterm (2 hours)   +   40% Final Exam (3 hours)
34% from 2 quizzes and 4 homework papers

Among 15 students, there seems to be 2 A+ students and 1 A student who got quite high marks in all quizzes and exams.

It seems not that difficult to get good grades or even full marks for all homework, quizzes and exams, if you are not that poor in math concepts and proofs. Some of the questions may simply ask for proof in the notes.
sections.workload:
Since students usually don't have much things to do, this course is not that time-consuming. Just take all classes, spend 2-3 hours a week for revision, 3-6 hours a week for homework, that seems enough. If you prefer to learn through textbook, that may take more time.

If you like to explore more, there are course materials from MATH3131 on the course webpage. You can check that.

sections.content:
I personally really liked the content of the course.
Mainly decided into 3 parts:
1. Basic Math Revision (Sets, Relations, Functions, Binary Operations, Complex Numbers)
2. Group Theory (Groups, Subgroups, Cyclic Groups, Permutations, Lagrange Theorem, Homomorphisms, Factor Groups, Group Action)
3. Ring Theory (Rings, Fields, Integral Domains, Fermat's Theorems)

However, I found it helpful to hear his explanations. Just helps revise concepts and important theorems for the exams.
